findings.quote: Second: a motor is supplied with 400 J and transfers 100 J usefully. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
findings.what: The lesson opens with an efficiency calculation that assumes an earlier lesson and is never used again here. Efficiency and its equation are not explained, so a first-time learner could fail the second question before the topic has begun.

findings.quote: One watt is one joule every second. So how many watts is 60 joules every second?
findings.what: "1 watt is 1 joule every second" was said in 1.5 immediately before. It is said again in this hint and again in every reply to 1.6 ("A watt is a joule each second").

findings.quote: Yes: watts. 1 W is 1 J each second.
findings.what: The same fact about the watt is repeated again, in identical words on every branch of this quiz question.

findings.quote: transfer the same energy, but the faster crane has four times the power
findings.what: "Four times" is asserted with no reasoning. The lesson file's step (the time is divided by 4, so the power is multiplied by 4) is missing, and she has not yet used P = E ÷ t to see why.

findings.quote: Two motors lift the same load to the same height. Motor X takes 10 s and motor Y takes 20 s. Which is true?
findings.what: The message just before (1.8) gave the same case with cranes (same energy, the faster one has more power), and 1.4 already said "The faster kettle has twice the power" for a 2:1 time ratio. She only has to copy the pattern.

findings.quote: Which one transfers it faster? (same buttons)
findings.what: The hint asks "which one?" (answer: X) but the buttons are three statements, none of which is simply "X". The smaller question does not fit the buttons she is given.

findings.quote: Not quite: same load, same height, so the same energy.
findings.what: She has not been taught why the same load lifted to the same height needs the same energy (work done comes in key point 4). It was only asserted for the cranes in 1.8.

findings.quote: Yes, your line has it: the energy transferred each second (the rate of energy transfer); and watts.
findings.what: The reply is a pasted marking list, not a sentence. "; and watts" reads oddly and does not model a good one-line answer.

findings.quote: Worked example: A light bulb transfers 1800 J in 3 minutes. What is its power?
findings.what: The very first worked example for P = E ÷ t already includes a minutes-to-seconds conversion. The lesson file starts with the plain case (100 J in 10 s), which is left out, so she never sees the equation used cleanly first.

findings.quote: Power stations are measured in megawatts (MW)
findings.what: It is the power output of a power station that is measured, not the power station. 3.2 then says a large power station gives out gigawatts, which sits oddly with this. Megawatts are also never used in any question.

findings.quote: To find the energy, rearrange to E = P × t. To find the time, t = E ÷ P. If you are unsure, put the numbers into P = E ÷ t first, then rearrange.
findings.what: Two new rearranged equations and a fallback method arrive in one message. "Rearrange" has no object until the last sentence, and how to rearrange is never shown.

findings.quote: To find the time, t = E ÷ P.
findings.what: There is no worked example for either rearranged form. The lesson file's heater example (t = 36 000 ÷ 2000 = 18 s) is omitted, so she goes straight to questions 2.6 and 2.7 cold.

findings.quote: A 2 kW heater is on for 30 s. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?
findings.what: The conversion this question tests was given with the same appliance and number in 2.3 ("A 2 kW heater has a power of 2000 W"). It is also her first try at E = P × t, with a unit conversion stacked on top.

findings.quote: Yes, your line has it: power in watts; and energy in joules; and time in seconds.
findings.what: Again the reply is a marking list joined with "; and", not a sentence a pupil would read naturally.

findings.quote: a kettle 2000 to 3000 W
findings.what: The lesson says kettles are 2000 to 3000 W, but its own questions use a 1.5 kW kettle (2.8 and 4.16). A sharp pupil would notice the mismatch.

findings.quote: Which of these transfers energy fastest?
findings.what: The two messages just before gave the kettle, the car motor and the power station with their sizes, including "A gigawatt is 1 000 000 000 W". The answer has just been read out to her.

findings.quote: Giga is bigger than mega, and mega is bigger than kilo. Which button has giga?
findings.what: The hint turns the question into spotting a word on a button. She can get it right with no idea of what power means.

findings.quote: s is the distance moved along the line of the force in metres (m)
findings.what: "Along the line of the force" is never explained. A 15-year-old meeting this for the first time will not know it means the distance moved in the direction the force acts.

findings.quote: W is the work done in joules (J), F is the force in newtons (N) and s is the distance
findings.what: Until now W meant watts and s meant seconds. Here W becomes work done and s becomes distance, with no warning that the same letters are being reused. "F s" is also written with no times sign, unlike every earlier equation.

findings.quote: W = 60 000 J, which is 60 kJ.
findings.what: The kilojoule has not been introduced. She has only met kilo in kilowatts.

findings.quote: Yes, that's right: 60000 J.
findings.what: The number is written without the space used everywhere else (60 000 J). This is a small inconsistency.

findings.quote: Lifting a box fills its gravitational potential store. Pushing a box against friction warms the box and the floor, so the energy goes to thermal stores.
findings.what: "Stores", "gravitational potential store" and "thermal stores" all appear in one message with no explanation, and "fills" is loose wording. Three ideas are told at once and no question ever checks them.

findings.quote: P is the power in watts (W), W is the work done in joules (J)
findings.what: W is used for watts and for work done in the same sentence with no comment. This is exactly where a beginner mixes up the unit and the quantity.

findings.quote: Yes, your line has it: the energy transferred when a force moves something (W = F s); and power is work done divided by time.
findings.what: The reply is a marking list, not a sentence. The question is also two questions in "one line".

findings.quote: Not quite: watts. 1 W is 1 J each second.
findings.what: The reply is identical for "Joules" and "Newtons". It does not tell her what the unit she chose actually measures, as the reply in 1.1a did.

findings.quote: Not quite: 4 minutes. Half the power transfers the same energy in twice the time.
findings.what: The same reply is given for "1 minute" and "2 minutes". Neither addresses her actual mistake (halving the time, or thinking power makes no difference).

findings.quote: Button: Next
findings.what: There is nothing hands-on anywhere: no picture, no widget, nothing to try. Every step is either read-and-tap-Next or type a number.

findings.quote: She types a number.
findings.what: Long runs of near-identical plug-in calculations with nothing interactive or visual. A pupil like Mabel is likely to get bored and switch off.

overall: Not quite as it stands, though it is close: the physics is sound and the order (kettles, rate, power, watt, equation) is sensible. Before she uses it I would fix the symbol clash in key point 4, where W is both watts and work done and s is both seconds and distance, and explain "along the line of the force" and the energy stores. I would also add a worked example for E = P × t and t = E ÷ P, give the reason for the crane's "four times", and replace or re-word the questions whose answers were given just before them (1.9, 3.3). The irrelevant efficiency starter should go, and with no picture or hands-on activity anywhere the lesson risks boring her.
